Meta understood the brain science behind why teens find ‌its platform so irresistible, Cartmell said.

Cartmell showed the jury an internal document from 2017 in which Meta product managers wrote that features like notifications and infinite scroll "are inherently at odds with well-being" and said that the company needed to warn the public.

"This warning never came," Cartmell said.

BROADER LEGAL BATTLE OVER PLATFORMS

Kevin Huff, a lawyer for Meta, said documents like those Cartmell cited are proof that the company is searching for problems on its platforms, so it can improve them.

The company has developed tools to help limit problematic use of Instagram, and seeks to empower teachers and parents to help ‌keep teens safe, Huff said.

Huff urged jurors to consider whether Meta should bear sole ​responsibility for societal problems such as suicide, child exploitation and addiction. "We think the evidence ​will show that Meta is doing its part and empowering others ​to do their part, because protecting teens online is a shared responsibility. It takes a village."

Nearly every state in ‌the country has filed claims against Meta over its platforms' ​alleged impact on children. More than ​two dozen of the lawsuits have been consolidated in multidistrict litigation in San Francisco, while many other states have sued in their own courts. Separately, Meta and other social media companies are facing thousands of lawsuits brought by individuals and school districts.

Tennessee's lawsuit is the ​second state case to reach a jury. Earlier ‌this year, a jury in New Mexico found the company liable and ordered it to pay $375 million. A judge is weighing ​additional financial penalties as well as an order directing the company to change Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp in the state.

title: How Apple Might Try to Make Its Smart Glasses Less Creepy
description: Apple's first pair of smart glasses is expected in 2027, giving the company a year to figure out how avoid the social stigma of Meta's glasses.
fullText:
Apple is expected to reveal its smart glasses, codename N50, at WWDC 17 in June 2027, which gives the company nearly a year to wrestle with the thorniest problem facing smart glasses: how do you uphold a commitment to privacy while selling a product that contains a hidden camera?

Like industry leader Meta's line of Ray-Ban and Oakley glasses, Apple's first smart glasses are expected to focus on AI, audio, and onboard cameras (display models are expected at a later date.) But Meta's glasses are at the center of a growing cultural firestorm for the camera feature, with people calling Metas "pervert glasses," creating guerrilla marketing campaigns against them, and banning them from a growing number of locations.

According to a Bloomberg report from Mark Gurman, Apple is considering releasing smart glasses with a full camera system that can't be used to take pictures or record video. The camera system would be used only for feeding visual information to Apple's AI tools, with no way for users to share that information.

Privacy (either respecting or exploiting) is no doubt at the forefront of every smart glass manufacturer's design decisions, but it's a particularly thorny issue for Apple, given its carefully cultivated image as "privacy first" company. Apple has spent years making data security a pillar of its identity, whether by repeatedly publicly proclaiming it as a "fundamental human right" or stressing on-device processing. Releasing a pair of glasses many would regard as spy glasses could effectively undermine Apple's reputation, even if every other privacy option (no sharing content with third parties, as much on-device processing as possible, etc.) is as robust as possible.

This isn't the first time Apple has been here. When it launched AirTags in 2021, the company built in anti-stalking features like unwanted-tracker alerts, audible chirps, and tools to locate a hidden tag, all to prevent the device from being used to secretly monitor people. But within months, the devices were reported in stalking and domestic abuse cases, prompting lawsuits, news investigations, and the general view of AirTags as tools for creeps. The lesson: good intentions and good engineering are no match for people's worst instincts.

According to consumer research, taking quick videos and pictures is one of the primary reasons people are buying smart glasses in the first place: a February 2026 Counterpoint Research report highlights that enhanced video performance and photography are the most frequently praised features of the Gen 2 Meta glasses. If consumers are facing a decision between Meta glasses, soon-to-be-released Samsung/Google smart glasses, and Apple glasses, how many would choose the one that doesn't have a camera?

While I have no idea what other possible solutions to the privacy problem Apple is considering, if I had to guess, I'd say they've discussed these ideas:

Geofencing: Apple could proactively build geofencing or detection agreements with categories of space like courts, gyms, and schools, or provide some kind of opt-in "fence" for users, like an iPhone setting for "no hidden cameras within my home/business." Given the ban of camera glasses in specific places like New York courts and sections of cruise ships, this seems like a strong contender for where things are headed.

Highly visible status light: Some of the backlash Meta has faced for its camera glasses is over the size of its tiny "I'm taping" warning light. What if it was bigger, brighter, and more visible? I could see that satisfying some people that don't wear and don't like smart glasses with cameras, but how many users want to advertise that they're wearing smart glasses?

A warning system for non-glasses users: There is already an app that tries to warn users if a pair of Meta glasses is in the vicinity; Apple could take the same idea and make it easy for anyone who cares to see who is wearing a pair of Apple glasses around them. Maybe this would even work as advertising, although again, I doubt glasses wearers would like to be singled out like this.

Count on this to blow over: Apple may decide it doesn't care about privacy that much after all; it wouldn't be the first time a company ditched a core value in favor of making a lot of money. Since there's more than a year until Apple glasses are expected to hit shelves, the company might just hope for the best. Public attitudes tend to get less alarmist over time as more people get used to new technology; when camera-equipped cell phones hit the market in the early 2000s, there was widespread panic over photography in gym locker rooms and schools, but that's not something anyone worries as much about these days.

title: Gianni Infantino Lashes Out at World Cup Critics
description: The FIFA president ripped the media in an Instagram post.
fullText:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino posted a 15-slide message directed at people “busy planting seeds of hate” on Instagram on Sunday night, claiming the World Cup went off without incident.

Infantino’s Sunday night missive began: “To everyone who missed our beautiful game…sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all.” He went on to further single out people “behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumours.”

The post was filled with jarring and inaccurate claims; he wrote that the World Cup saw “zero incidents, zero hostility, zero violence, just joy, emotions, happiness, unity, and togetherness.”

Four people died during celebrations in Mexico City after Mexico beat Ecuador in the round of 32. South African midfielder Jayden Adams was found dead in Cape Town after returning from the tournament, and police are investigating a cause of death.

FIFA did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the inaccuracies or what prompted Infantino’s post.

Even and especially at its best, the World Cup—as always—stirred up hostility and political tensions. Argentine fans in Atlanta were captured on video fighting with one another on the night before the match, and with England fans after the semifinal win. The match reignited historic claims from the Argentine government, players, and fans against Great Britain over the Falkland Islands, including with an on-pitch demonstration by the players. In the U.K., more domestic abuse incidents were reported during the tournament than the past two World Cups and Euros.

Infantino also wrote that “Iran entered the United States without incident or conflict.” Iran’s coach, though, said his side was “perhaps the most oppressed” team in the tournament after the quick trip from Tijuana to Los Angeles took five hours with security screenings, then the team would need to return immediately after the match. Iran saw 11 federation members and team staffers denied entry into the U.S., including federation president Mehdi Taj.

The Iranian federation also said it would file a complaint to FIFA for denying its request to travel two days in advance of its match against Belgium.

Infantino wrote that “Football is bigger than hate and discrimination.” Multiple incidents of racist abuse occurred during the World Cup. Most notably, a Paraguayan senator called Kylian Mbappé a “colonised Cameroonian,” to which the French captain called her “a despicable woman and unworthy of your position.”

Infantino said the World Cup’s haters “mentioned the few people denied visas and overlooked the millions who were approved, from all parts of the world.”

The most high profile visa cases include that of Somali referee Omar Artan, denied entry into the U.S. over alleged “association with suspected members of terrorist organizations,” and Ghana midfielder Thomas Partey, who was not allowed into Canada for matches due to ongoing rape charges.

And fans from Haiti, Iran, Senegal, and Ivory Coast were simply banned from entering the United States under blanket Trump administration policy; others were subject to a $15,000 bond that deterred many from coming. (FIFA celebrated that it got the U.S. to waive this requirement, but that only applied to a certain subset of fans who had already purchased tickets and opted into an expedited visa process.)

Infantino did not mention Folarin Balogun’s red card or its subsequent suspension directly, but he was still defensive about the notorious incident.

“Indeed, ‘arguable’ referees’ decisions or ‘strange’ disciplinary rulings such as for instance potentially mistaken red or yellow cards or subsequent decisions not to ban players in certain situations are routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide,” Infantino wrote. “It’s curious that the same countries employing these practices are the ones criticising.”

European leaders had blasted FIFA’s handlingof Balogun’s red card to the point where UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin—whose organization called the red card reversal an “unprecedented, incomprehensible and unjustifiable decision”—boycotted the tournament final. (Some European leagues do review red cards after games, which is not generally FIFA protocol.)

Infantino has not taken questions from reporters since a press conference before the opening match in Mexico City on June 10.

There, Infantino was also defensive and vague, saying, “We try to do our best” on a number of issues like Iran, high ticket prices, and visa restrictions. After initially telling people to “chill, relax,” Infantino later clarified that he meant “to trust us that we are working behind the scenes.”

He was more aggressive on Sunday night.

“To those spending their time and energy hating us, please take a moment to reflect, meditate, pray, or watch a football match and truly observe the faces, the eyes, the emotions,” Infantino wrote. “To the pens and papers, to all the screens, may you find love and peace where the people behind you couldn’t.

“May you find peace; we at FIFA have found ours and we deliver it, by delivering the most outstanding FIFA World Cup.”

Also on Sunday night, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D., MD) sent Infantino a letter asking for a list of any money or gifts exchanged between FIFA and anyone related to President Trump, and visitor logs at the governing body’s Miami and New York offices. FIFA houses its New York office in Trump Tower. The Athletic first reported news of the letter.

Raskin also asked Infantino to appear before the House Judiciary Committee, of which he is the ranking member.

The post Gianni Infantino Lashes Out at World Cup Critics appeared first on Front Office Sports.

title: A Teen Reporter Searched for His Community in the Epstein Files. Adults Freaked
description: An Instagram post turned one California student newspaper into a free-speech flash point. The students say they were just doing their homework.
fullText:
for his journalism class was to tell a news story—any news story—in the form of an extended Instagram slideshow. So when the high school senior got home on the afternoon of February 10, 2026, he grabbed a snack, went upstairs to his room, and settled in to work.

After allowing himself a few minutes of procrastination—scouting prospective college campuses on Google Earth—Mueller navigated over to the Department of Justice’s Epstein Library portal and clicked through the page asking whether he was 18 or older (he was, just barely). Then he began poking around for ideas in the 3 million pages of Epstein files that had been added 11 days earlier.

Mueller really liked working in his bedroom, with its beanbag chair and view of people strolling and biking along one of Marin County, California’s sun-dappled waterways. Having lived his whole life in one of the wealthiest parts of America, Mueller couldn’t help thinking his area probably had some ties to Jeffrey Epstein. “I think it’s very difficult to get an immense amount of money without—this is my opinion—without doing something a little shady,” Mueller says. So he sat on his bedroom floor and spent the next five hours combing the federal database for links to the towns and cities of Marin.

He found thousands. Most of them were trivial (Epstein liked to shop online at Restoration Hardware, headquartered in nearby Corte Madera). But a few things stood out: a 2014 art gala in Sausalito that Epstein helped promote; a meeting with Woody Allen in Tiburon; and—above all—a 2013 email exchange between Epstein and an address bearing the name of a woman associated with a French model casting agency called Mill Valley Connection. “Regarding Hannah, my Austrian model,” read one particularly chilling message, “we can come and see you this evening if you are interested, and in that case let me know how I can get my fees.”

Two days later, on February 12, Mueller posted his story to the Instagram feed of the Redwood Bark, his school’s student-run publication. It was a carousel-style slideshow pitched at readers across the county. “Which Marin towns were mentioned in the Epstein files?” the first panel reads. “Scroll to see how many times your town was mentioned.” Rather than quote from the most alarming document he’d found, Mueller kept his descriptions fairly general and brief: “Mill Valley was mentioned in the context of providing models to Epstein from a woman named Gisele Attias Bonnouvrier.”

More than 4,000 people liked the story. The comments filled up with praise: “This is the kind of journalism we need.” “Higher quality reporting than local outlets.” “High schoolers doing better reporting than national news.” “Didn’t think I’d be following a random CA HS newspaper in 2026 for their breaking reporting but here we are.”

As Mueller watched the numbers climb, he felt excited but also a little perplexed. “I didn’t really think I was doing groundbreaking journalism,” he says. “I was just like, this is another piece of homework that I have to do today, and I’ve just got to get it done—but also be thorough, because people are going to see it on the internet.”

About a week and a half later, Mueller was home sick with a light fever and cough when the phone rang. It was his journalism teacher, Erin Schneider, with bad news. “This person mentioned in your post is now threatening to sue the district,” she said.

On Monday, February 23, Bonnouvrier, the woman affiliated with the model casting agency, had sent an email to the principal of Redwood High School, calling Mueller’s post defamatory, demanding its immediate removal, and promising legal action if the school did not comply within 48 hours. And now the district superintendent was demanding that the Bark either redact Bonnouvrier’s name or delete the slide entirely.

title: Instagram Is Starting to Crack Down on Creepy Smart Glasses Videos
description: Creepy videos are being more heavily scrutinized by Meta.
fullText:
In a recent story posted on Instagram, Instagram head Adam Mosseri revealed the social media platform is banning smart glasses videos where people are being harassed and exploited for views.

"If you're posting content that is taking advantage of people and harassing them, like a lot of these pickup line kind of videos that we've heard of and seen, then we're going to take the content down," Mosseri said. "We don't want people to be surreptitiously taking videos of other people and harassing them and then posting them on our platform. So we're trying to fight that every way we can."

Hidden camera prank videos and "pickup" type videos are obviously not new, but the easy availability of camera glasses has led to a spike in this kind of content, with videos of men trying to pick up women, pranking retail workers, and other pranks appearing more frequently across all video-sharing services.

Business Insider reported that Meta recently pulled two accounts with over a million followers for posting "pickup artist" videos, where women who may not have known they were being filmed have their videos posted online, leading to harassment. A Meta spokesperson confirmed that the accounts were nuked in accordance with the company's existing bullying and harassment policy.

Meta's official policy on bullying states "We remove content that's meant to degrade or shame, including, for example, claims about someone's sexual activity," and lists a number of specific examples like, "severe sexualized commentary" and "calls for, or statements of intent to engage in, bullying and/or harassment." But there's a lot of gray area. Videos featuring vaguely aggressive acts directed at strangers apparently aren't in violation of Meta's standards, for instance. Neither is a video like the one below, but I'd feel pretty harassed if I were that doctor.

There isn't a reliable way to automate harassment detection because so much of what constitutes harassment comes down to intent and context. This leaves enforcement up to users who can flag videos and/or victims, who are often unaware their image is being spread online until it's too late to put the toothpaste back in the tube.

The backlash over camera-equipped smart glasses is definitely growing, whether its apps designed to suss them out in public, condemnation from pop stars, or outright bans on smart glasses in some places.

As a privacy safeguard, Meta's glasses have a front-facing light that comes on when video is being taken or a picture is being snapped, but the light has been an ongoing issue since the glasses launched. Disabling it has turned into an ongoing game of cat-and-mouse: Meta smart glasses' cameras won't work if the light is covered, but hackers found ways to modify the hardware itself, leading Meta to release a mandatory update that will physically disable any glasses if a user tampers with the indicator. Creeps are pretty ingenious, so I expect further workarounds.

Whether they have lights or not, hidden cameras are generally legal to use in public places in the U.S. (with a few exceptions), and it's not necessarily against the law to film yourself trying to pick someone up, then post the footage online so weirdos can comment, either.

Unless you're really eagle-eyed, it's tough to spot someone with a hacked pair of glasses with no recording indicator light, but it's not impossible. Here are a few things to look for:

The rivet: Most standard glasses have decoration of some kind to cover the glasses' hinge. On Meta Ray-Bans and most other camera glasses, they're round and slightly oversized with a glass inner circle.

Thick frames: While the technology is getting smaller, camera equipped glasses tend to have thicker frames to hide the gear.

The tap: There's two ways to trigger an off-the-shelf pair of Meta smart glasses, saying "Hey, Meta, take video" or tapping the side of the glasses.

Head movement: Meta glasses have a pretty wide lens, so they don't require a ton of movement to capture a scene, but still, if someone is moving their head when they could just be moving their eyes, they might be trying to keep something in frame.

All that said, despite the growing popularity of the nickname "pervert glasses," camera-equipped smart glasses have a variety of legitimate uses and I assume the vast majority of wearers want a quick way to upload content to Instagram, answer texts, or take a picture without having to pull out their phones, so just spotting the glasses in the wild doesn't mean you've spotted a creeper. Usually.

title: You Can Now Verify Your Facebook Account With a Video Selfie
description: Upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark. But is that a good idea?
fullText:
If you're on Facebook, you may soon see a new type of verification badge on user profiles meant to indicate that there is a real, live person behind them. The platform is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark, which will appear on their profile and across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups. (At launch, badges won't appear in Feed posts, but Facebook says that feature will be added in the future.)

Note that this is different from Meta Verified, a paid subscription that provides the blue check mark to accounts on Facebook and Instagram. This verification indicates that Meta has confirmed the user's identity based on a review of their government-issued ID and, in some cases, a selfie video.

Facebook Verified is available to users age 18 and older whose accounts are in good standing with the platform's community standards, though the feature is launching in select markets initially before being rolled out globally. Once you have access, you'll need to record a short video selfie, which Facebook will compare to existing profile photos on your account using facial recognition. If your verification is approved, the white check mark will be added to your profile. Verification is not available for Pages or ProMode accounts.

Facebook says it will store your selfie video for "up to 30 days" after verification, which is a one-time process. It's not entirely clear what happens with that video in the meantime, and it's worth noting that Meta has relied on user data to train its AI. Meta AI (and Meta more broadly) is a terrible offender when it comes to privacy and security, so you should consider whether the tradeoff of a verification mark is worth handing over more of your data and read the privacy policy before you agree.

Google also launched a video selfie verification feature this week, though its purpose is to prove your identity should you get locked out of your account. Unlike Facebook Verified, which is meant to be a trust signal to other users, Google's selfie verification allows access to your entire Google account, bringing with it some additional security considerations.

title: This App Can Help Detect When Someone Near You Is Wearing Meta Glasses
description: But it only detects them when they are charging, powering on, or while they're actively pairing.
fullText:
An app has launched that detects whether the people around you are using Meta and other kinds of smart glasses. Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner, available for iPhone and designed by Albert Pariente Cohen, detects nearby Bluetooth signals that match Meta glasses, Snap Spectacles, Meta Quest headsets, RayNeo smart glasses, and other devices; then, it lets you know what gadget is nearby and whether it's been detected previously. In keeping with the "privacy" focus, Antizuck doesn't require an account or email address, nor does it send any data outside of your phone. It retails for $2.99 with no subscription.

In my testing, Antizuck successfully identified both my Meta glasses and my Quest 3 headset. It actually called out my Quest 3 (name and distance) while the headset was in sleep mode. The Meta glasses, though, weren't as easily detected. While it did find my glasses, it only "saw" them when I turned them off and on: Antizuck only detects Meta glasses that are charging, powering on, or while they're actively pairing.

The app can also tell you all the other Bluetooth devices advertising around you, and it identifies what they are, if possible. Interestingly, it identified my charging Even Realities G2 smart glasses, but didn't flag them, I assume because they don't have a camera. Still, just seeing how many devices are broadcasting around you is worth the $3 price of admission.

It's clear from the app's "glasses spotted" warning of "Someone may be recording near you" that the point is to let you know if a creep is creeping nearby, but they're only marginally useful for that purpose. They do not let you know which passersby are wearing Meta glasses. They don't show you an alert when a nearby pair of glasses starts recording or takes a picture, nor do they alert you when a nearby pair of Meta glasses is transferring media from the glasses to a phone. If someone turns on their glasses near you or charges them for three minutes or so, you'll get a ping and a record of whether that same pair of glasses has been detected by you in the past. But most people aren't charging their glasses on a street corner or in a bar.

Utility aside, the app is clearly part of the growing backlash against people using camera-forward smart glasses, whether it's New York banning them in court, or singer Lorde calling them "not sexy." I completely understand the concern people, particularly women, have about being recorded by hidden spy glasses, but it's not as one-sided an argument as it may appear at first. People with vision problems use Meta glasses to get verbal help from the AI. Birdwatchers use them to identify birds on the fly. I use my Meta glasses to categorize receipts for tax purposes, listen to Hawkwind, and occasionally take videos on bike rides. I'd rather not have strangers assume I'm a creep, or know that I'm wearing a specific brand of eyeglasses at all. Just as it's legal to take photos in public places, it's legal to scan your surroundings for Bluetooth signatures, but isn't each an invasion of privacy? Like anything, the only thing evil about a tool is how you use it.

title: ‘Call us whatever the hell you want’: Mark Zuckerberg just launched an AI optimism blitz using nostalgia to sell Meta’s AI future amid backlash
description: Marketing experts say Meta invokes Facebook-era optimism while leaving recent AI lawsuits and product backlash unaddressed.
fullText:
In a week where an AI model went rogue and broke out of a secure test environment—and in a year where seemingly all we're hearing is how AI can displace large swaths of the workforce—it may come as a surprise when one of the tech's most prominent voices is pushing an optimistic view of the tech, joining the many in his field who have recently walked back comments of how it could negatively impact workers.

What recent controversies is Meta facing with AI?

How effective is nostalgic marketing for AI concerns?

Why is Meta using nostalgia to market AI?

How are AI leaders walking back job displacement fears?

"As we enter this next wave with AI, we continue to believe the future is for everyone," Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote as the caption to a short video on Thursday, harkening back to the company's early years of tech optimism.

"Call us optimists, call us dreamers, call us whatever the hell you want, but we're betting on people, and we like those odds," the voiceover in the video said.

The video featured montages of people using Instagram, Whatsapp, FaceBook and Meta's Ray-Ban glasses to film touching moments and connect with loved ones, with the backdrop of concerts and snowboarding and laughing children set to calm music as the voiceover framed Meta's AI efforts as doubling down on betting on people, just like the company did 22 years ago with FaceBook.

Marketing experts told Fortune that the Meta video's reliance on nostalgic imagery seemed like a way to redirect attention from AI concerns and to buffer against growing AI fears.

"They're showing people having a great time, but they're not really responding to what the fundamental issue is, which is how is AI going to impact me when I start dealing with your platform when you integrate all of that technology into it," Mara Einstein, a media studies professor at CUNY's Queens College, told Fortune. "The problem is the AI technology is not the same as previous versions of social media that they have used to connect people in the past."

The sentiment was echoed by Ana Babic Rosario, a marketing professor at the University of Denver's Daniels College of Business, who pointed to Meta's more recent struggles as reason why Meta might want to draw nostalgia to the past. Last week, Meta employees sued the company for allegedly using AI in the company's recent 8,000 layoffs that the employees claim disproportionately targeted workers on medical, parental or family leave. Employees at Meta's Applied AI unit also compared working conditions at the company to a "gulag" and the tasks "soul crushing." The company also scrapped an AI-generated images pilot on Instagram, and is facing a lawsuit on its Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

YouTube and TikTok ‌settled in June and Snap reached a tentative settlement in the case, Bloomberg ‌reported on Monday. The terms of those settlements were confidential.

RKC, who started using social media when he was about eight, said he became addicted to it, losing sleep and suffering from depression and anxiety, according ‌to court filings.

“In light of the overall successful result of the litigation and his concerns about ​enduring a grueling weeks-long trial, he has elected to withdraw his claims against Meta,” attorneys for RKC said in a statement. “He’s ready to close this chapter and focus on his recovery ⁠and engage in therapy as he aspires to have a ​normal life.”

A ​spokesperson for Meta said RKC had dropped the claims ​without receiving ‌any payment.

“The claims ​never held ​up,” the company said in a statement. This outcome makes clear that we will not back away from defending ourselves against baseless lawsuits.”

The dropped case comes after Meta and YouTube suffered a bruising loss in March in the same Los Angeles court. That trial lasted six weeks and ended with the two companies being ordered to pay a young woman $6m in damages. In the landmark decision, the jury found Meta and YouTube liable for deliberately designing addictive products and negligent for having failed to provide adequate warnings about the potential dangers of their platforms.

In a separate lawsuit in March brought by New Mexico’s attorney general, a jury ordered Meta to pay $375m in civil penalties over claims that it misled consumers about the safety of its platforms and enabled harm, including child sexual exploitation, against its users. The back-to-back verdicts are the first ever to find social media companies liable for how their products affect young people.

These cases were the first to go to court, and are slated to be followed by more trials from two coordinated groups of more than 2,000 plaintiffs, including families, school districts and state attorneys general, who have brought lawsuits against Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap.

The four social media companies also settled another major lawsuit just before trial in May, brought by a school district in Kentucky over similar claims of addictive products leading to harm in children.

This month, Meta appealed the verdict in its loss at the Los Angeles court. It challenged the jury’s decision that found the company liable for designing addictive products to hook in young people.

Meta and the other social media companies have vigorously defended their business models, saying their products aren’t addictive. In a post on Wednesday, Andy Stone, Meta’s communications director, wrote that RKC’s claims “never held up” and that he “averaged just minutes a day on Facebook and Instagram”.

Lawyers for RKC said they achieved what they set out to do by bringing awareness to social media’s alleged harms.

“RKC came into this process wanting to hold social media companies accountable and push for changes to protect young people like himself,” the lawyers said. “He did that.”
